article.overview: A sample curation container is a sealed, clean container that holds extraterrestrial material from the moment it is collected until it is opened in a controlled laboratory. Its main job is not to measure anything. It protects the sample from contamination, loss and changes to its physical state during collection, launch, transit, return and handling. NASA's curation office describes curation as the documentation, preservation, preparation, and distribution of samples for research, education, and public outreach. The best-documented example is the Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container (ALSRC), an aluminium box with a triple seal between its body and lid. Later sample-return programmes, including Luna 16 (1970), Chang'e-5 (2020) and Chang'e-6 (2024), also carried material in sealed containers of their own. There is no single standard design for this payload class.
article.description: A sample container is a rigid body with a lid, a sealing interface, an internal mounting or liner for the sample, and a method for controlling the gas inside. For lunar material the container must hold its sealed condition through launch and transit and then be opened without contaminating the sample. The Apollo ALSRC is the most fully described example. According to a Y-12 history article quoting a 1973 completion report, the body was machined from a single piece of aluminium, so it had no welds or seams. The lid was made the same way, so the only potential leak path was the lid-to-body seal. A 1988 conference paper on lunar sampling tools states that the ALSRCs used one indium seal and two Viton seals, and that interior container pressures measured on return to the laboratory showed these seals were not reliable in the lunar environment. The same paper notes that the indium seal interfered with siderophile element analyses. Human-factor testing and astronaut training led to many changes in the design of the hand tools and of the ALSRC, especially its latching and sealing hardware.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: A sample container serves three purposes. First, it preserves chemistry: Apollo hardware had to be cleaned so that residual organic contamination from Earth could not interfere with parts-per-billion analysis of lunar samples. Second, it preserves physical state: the ALSRC was designed to keep vacuum during the trans-lunar part of the mission and after it was resealed on the lunar surface. Third, it enables later analysis: the Chang'e-5 samples that reached France were stored in glass vials inside an aluminium container, and researchers used X-ray computed tomography to measure the container and sample volumes before any opening. A gas extraction from the container base into an ultra-high-vacuum bottle was planned; this describes planned curation work in a 2025 conference abstract, not a completed result. Distribution is also part of the purpose: typical research subsamples from the Apollo collection weigh 0.5 to 1 gram.
article.operating_principle: A sample container has no sensing principle. Its operating principle is containment. It works by sealing the sample from the outside environment through a compressed seal between a body and a lid (the Apollo ALSRC used a triple seal); by controlling the internal atmosphere, with Apollo's design goal being to retain vacuum and later curation cabinets using nitrogen; by protecting the sample mechanically with a mount or liner; and by controlled opening in a laboratory built for that purpose. A 2019 article reports that NASA's Apollo sample cabinets are pressurised with pure nitrogen at a pressure above the surrounding room, which pushes debris away from the samples. The Smithsonian object record for an ALSRC describes an aluminium mesh liner that absorbs shock; this was not verified in this review.
article.scientific_importance: Lunar samples cannot be replaced, so the container is part of the scientific record. NASA's curation office notes that the six Apollo landings returned about 2,200 samples with a total mass of 382 kg, and that curation starts as soon as a sample-return mission is conceived. The Apollo ALSRC shows how container choices affect science: the 1988 paper found that the seals did not hold reliably and that the indium seal interfered with some chemical analyses. Any future container must therefore be judged by its effect on both containment and analytical chemistry.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a sample curation container. Container design depends on the mission's sample type, its return environment and its laboratory. For most containers reviewed here, the sources do not publish dimensions, mass or power. Values are reported only where a source states them, and unlike designs are not compared directly.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container (ALSRC)
examples.construction: Single-piece aluminium body and lid with a triple seal between them. Y-12 supplied the containers, and a Y-12 historian reports two boxes on each flight.
examples.seals: One indium seal and two Viton seals. Interior pressures measured on return suggested the seals were not reliable in the lunar environment.
examples.design_drivers: Human-factor testing and astronaut training shaped the latching and sealing hardware.
examples.qualification: Dimensions, mass and power were not publicly specified in the sources read for this article. The Smithsonian object record was not accessible in this review.

examples.name: Chang'e-5 sample container
examples.construction: CNSA stated in December 2020 that the samples were stowed in a container inside the ascender and sealed to keep them in a vacuum. The samples reached France stored in glass vials inside an aluminium container.
examples.seals: Vacuum sealing described by CNSA; seal design not specified in the sources read.
examples.qualification: Container dimensions, mass and seal design were not specified in the sources read.

examples.name: Chang'e-6 sealed sample container
examples.construction: A sealed sample container carried in the ascender. A 5 June 2024 report says the ascender carried samples collected over two days in a sealed container and that it would transfer the sample-loaded container to the reentry capsule before undocking.
examples.seals: Not specified in the sources read.
examples.qualification: The transfer is described as a planned step in that report, not a completed one. Dimensions, mass and seal design were not specified in the sources read.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for the containers listed. Apollo ALSRC dimensions were not located in the sources read. The Smithsonian object record should be checked when it becomes accessible.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for the containers listed. Container mass is important for launch and lander planning, but none of the containers examined here has a verified mass figure in this article.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: A passive sealed container needs no electrical power. None of the sources reviewed describes a powered sample container. Any heated, cooled or instrumented container would need its own power budget, which is not covered here.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Contamination control: the Apollo sample collection is held in clean-room suites rated ISO class 6 and 7, and NASA routinely monitors inorganic and organic contamination in processing cabinets and weekly airborne particle counts. Inert gas: NASA's Johnson Space Center uses ultrapure dry gaseous nitrogen systems; each delivery of liquid nitrogen is monitored, with typical levels below 20 ppm argon and below 1 ppm of all others combined. Vacuum: the ALSRC was designed to retain vacuum before, during and after the lunar part of the mission. Thermal and radiation environment: the sources reviewed do not give container-level temperature or radiation requirements for these containers.
article.limitations: Seal reliability: pressure measurements on return showed that the Apollo ALSRC seals were not reliable in the lunar environment. Analytical interference: the indium seal interfered with siderophile element analyses. Single failure path: the Y-12 account identifies the lid-to-body seal as the only potential leak path in the ALSRC design, so any seal failure would compromise containment. Controlled opening: a sealed container must be opened in a controlled laboratory, which adds time and cost and limits field inspection. Missing specifications: the sources reviewed do not publish dimensions, mass or power for the Apollo, Luna 16, Chang'e-5 or Chang'e-6 containers.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: This is a sample-return payload. Its transportation concerns are containment, handling, sealing, transfer and the return chain.
transportation_process: Collection and sealing: Apollo ALSRCs were sealed on the lunar surface. Chang'e-5 samples were stowed in a container inside the ascender. Luna 16's drill column was transferred into a sealed soil container.
Lunar ascent and transfer: Chang'e-6's sample container was carried in the ascender and was to be transferred to the reentry capsule in lunar orbit (planned in a June 2024 report).
Return: the Apollo ALSRC design goal was to retain vacuum through the trans-lunar part of the mission. Luna 16 returned its soil sample in a sealed container inside a re-entry capsule.
Receiving: Y-12 built and managed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory, and its vacuum system was integrated with the ALSRC. The Apollo samples were later stored at JSC's building 31N, completed in 1978.

Distribution: a 2019 article reports that subsamples leave the laboratory by regular mail, FedEx or UPS in unmarked packaging and are not insured. This is a secondary report of current practice and may have changed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Sample containers are not deployed in the same sense as instruments. They are filled on the surface and then transported. Apollo ALSRCs were sealed on the lunar surface. The Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 handling methods are not described in sufficient detail in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo: ALSRCs returned about 2,200 samples from the six landings. Luna 16 (1970): a hermetically sealed soil container was returned from Mare Fecunditatis with about 101 g of soil. Chang'e-5 (2020) and Chang'e-6 (2024): sealed containers carried the samples through lunar ascent and return.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No container in this article has been verified for a specific lander or spacecraft. Compatibility would depend on mass, dimensions, mounting, sealing requirements, the return chain and the receiving laboratory. None of those has been verified for a named vehicle here.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo ALSRC programme established the sealed-container approach for returned lunar material. Apollo returned about 2,200 samples totalling 382 kg, and their curation has continued for decades. Y-12 also introduced Teflon to its work on the moon box, which it describes as the first Y-12 project to use that material. Luna 16 (1970) returned a sealed soil sample. Chang'e-5 (2020) and Chang'e-6 (2024) returned samples in sealed containers, with Chang'e-6 bringing back far-side material. These later missions show the same basic approach: seal the sample, keep it isolated, and open it in a controlled laboratory.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No verified dimensions, mass or power for any container in this article. Smithsonian object record not accessed: the airandspace.si.edu domain did not resolve and si.edu returned HTTP 403 during this review, so the reported 7075 aluminium case and 2024 aluminium mesh liner are not verified. The 1972 NASA technical report on Lunar Receiving Laboratory sample processing (NTRS 19720017449) is a scanned PDF whose text was not extracted; a 1976 NASA history PDF returned HTTP 404. The Science News (2019) article reports NASA staff quotes rather than primary curation records. The Luna 16 details come from Wikipedia. The Chang'e-6 report is a 2024 news article. The Chang'e-5 French curation results come from a 2025 conference abstract describing planned work. Only one image is verified and used; it is a training photograph, not a flight image.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Reference URLs have been checked for the absence of query strings and fragments.

data_quality_notes: Smithsonian object record for the Apollo 11 ALSRC (NASM A19710813000) was not accessed: airandspace.si.edu did not resolve and si.edu returned HTTP 403 during this review. The reported 7075 aluminium case, 2024 aluminium mesh liner and shock-absorbing mesh description are unverified and are not stated as facts in the article.
No verified dimensions, mass or power were found for the Apollo ALSRC or for any other container in this article. Fields are null or marked not specified.

The Y-12 article date (2009) is inferred from its text (it refers to the 40th anniversary of the landing) and from the PDF creation metadata (July 2009). The article itself does not state a publication date.
The Y-12 article quotes a 1973 completion report (Mundt, Schreyer and Wampler). The 1973 report itself was not read.

The 1972 NASA technical report on Lunar Receiving Laboratory sample processing (NTRS 19720017449) is a scanned PDF. Its text was not extracted, so the Apollo LRL sealed-container processing cabinet details it may contain are not used. A 1976 NASA history PDF (alsj 19760023161) returned HTTP 404.

A search summary of a NASA technical report mentioned a sterile nitrogen (SNAP) cabinet line installed in the Lunar Receiving Laboratory after Apollo 12. This was not verified from a primary text and is not stated in the article.

The Photojournal caption for PIA24297 was only partly visible in the fetched text. The wording 'lunar-surface simulation training exercise' and the Building 9 location are taken from the fetched Photojournal summary and a search summary; the photograph date (18 April 1969) is from the fetched page.
The Photojournal page carries a Mars 2020 catalogue tag. This is a cross-mission label, not evidence of Mars 2020 involvement in the Apollo-era photograph.
The Science News (2019) article author was not identified in the fetched text. Its claims about nitrogen cabinet pressure and debris are reported from NASA staff and are secondary.
Luna 16 details are from Wikipedia, a secondary source. The 101 g returned-sample figure should be checked against a primary Soviet or archival source before reuse.

Chang'e-6 details are from a June 2024 news report. The planned transfer to the reentry capsule is not confirmed as completed in the source. A reported returned-mass figure and a container capacity figure from secondary sites were excluded because they could not be verified against a primary source.

The Chang'e-5 French curation details (glass vials in an aluminium container, X-ray CT, planned gas extraction) come from a 2025 conference abstract describing planned work. The gas extraction was not confirmed as completed.
Only one image was verified. The image is a training photograph, not a flight image. No additional Apollo or Lunar Receiving Laboratory images were verified from official pages.
research_status.technical_specifications_fully_audited is false because most container dimensions, masses and seal designs for the non-Apollo examples could not be verified from primary sources.
Lander and spacecraft compatibility was not verified for any container. Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user and are not included.
